subtopic_detail: Older man with rooms impassable from accumulated possessions who feels distress only when others try to discard them and has no intrusive contamination thoughts
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a home visit on a 68 year old man after his daughter rang the practice. Newspapers, containers and unopened purchases are stacked to shoulder height through the hallway and only a narrow path remains to the kitchen, where the stove cannot be reached.

He tells you calmly that everything has a use and he will sort it when he has time, and he becomes visibly distressed only when his daughter suggests a skip bin. He describes no repetitive washing, checking or counting, and no intrusive thoughts he is trying to neutralise. His mood is reactive and he denies anhedonia. He scores 28 out of 30 on cognitive screening and manages his own finances and medications accurately.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and oriented, speech normal in rate and form, mood reactive with no psychomotor slowing, no delusional explanation offered for the accumulation, insight limited regarding the safety risk, Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a high dose and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: High dose serotonergic medication is the pharmacological approach to obsessive compulsive disorder, and the near pair matters because response rates in difficulty discarding are considerably lower. Medication is added when depression or anxiety coexists rather than as the primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for difficulty discarding
options.rationale: Persistent difficulty parting with possessions, distress at the thought of discarding, and clutter that prevents rooms from being used as intended defines a condition in its own right, and the treatment with the best evidence is a structured cognitive behavioural programme covering motivation, sorting skills and graded discarding. It outperforms generic therapy and is delivered over months. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a forced clean out by council officers with family present to remove the risk
options.rationale: Involuntary clearance reliably produces rapid re-accumulation and a rupture in the therapeutic relationship, and it is reserved for imminent and otherwise unmanageable danger. Even then it is coordinated with treatment rather than used instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment for a frontal lobe syndrome
options.rationale: Accumulation that begins abruptly in later life, especially with disinhibition, apathy or personality change, does warrant assessment for a frontotemporal process. His cognition screens normally and he continues to manage complex daily tasks. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hoarding disorder)

options.text: Refer to the aged care assessment team for placement in supported residential care
options.rationale: Residential placement addresses functional decline from cognitive or physical impairment, neither of which he has, and it does not treat the behaviour that produced the clutter. He manages his medications and finances independently. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Difficulty discarding possessions became a separate diagnosis because it differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in phenomenology, treatment response and course. The accumulation is driven by beliefs about usefulness, waste and emotional attachment rather than by intrusive thoughts that the person is trying to neutralise, and distress arises at the prospect of discarding rather than from the clutter itself. Insight is characteristically poor, which is why referral usually comes from family, neighbours or council rather than the person. Prevalence rises with age and the associated risks are substantial, including falls, fire, structural damage, infestation and eviction. Treatment is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural programme, often combined with practical in home support, and medication addresses comorbid depression or anxiety rather than the behaviour itself.
key_points: Distress arises at discarding, not from the clutter or from intrusive thoughts
Clutter must prevent rooms being used for their intended purpose
Insight is typically poor and referral usually comes from others
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is the primary treatment
Late onset accumulation with personality change suggests a frontal process
explanation.pearls: Forced clearance without concurrent psychological treatment is followed by re-accumulation to the previous level in the majority of cases within two years, so a skip bin arranged without therapy is a temporary fix that also destroys the working relationship needed for the real one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent girl with a widening area of missing scalp hair pulled out when studying, with relief afterwards and no scaling or broken hair of varying length on the rest of the scalp
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her mother because of a bald patch at the crown that has widened over six months. Her mother has noticed hair on the desk when she is studying for exams.

When you see her alone she tells you she pulls hairs out one at a time while she is concentrating or lying in bed, feels a build up of tension first and a sense of relief afterwards, and has tried to stop several times. She denies eating the hair. She is embarrassed and now wears her hair up to hide it. She is doing well at school, has friends, sleeps normally and denies low mood or thoughts of self harm. There are no intrusive thoughts and no rituals.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patch of hair loss at the crown measuring about 5 cm with hairs of varying lengths within it, no scaling, erythema, scarring or broken hair beyond the patch, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no palpable abdominal mass, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for pulling behaviours, unlike in obsessive compulsive disorder where they are central. They are reserved for coexisting depression or anxiety, neither of which she has. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid scalp lotion and review the patch in eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats an autoimmune patch of hair loss, which produces a smooth bald area with exclamation mark hairs at the margin rather than hairs of differing lengths within it. Her varying hair lengths indicate mechanical removal at different times. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Alopecia)

options.text: Prescribe oral terbinafine for four weeks after sending scalp scrapings for fungal culture
options.rationale: Fungal scalp infection gives scaling, broken hairs close to the skin and often occipital lymphadenopathy, and it is the near pair because both produce patchy loss in a young person. Her scalp skin is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for assessment of a possible gastric hair mass
options.rationale: Surgical referral is warranted when hair is swallowed, which produces abdominal pain, vomiting, a palpable mass or iron deficiency. She denies eating hair, her abdomen is normal and her iron studies are unremarkable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trichotillomania)

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training delivered by a trained psychologist over several sessions
options.rationale: Repetitive pulling with rising tension beforehand and relief afterwards, plus repeated failed attempts to stop, identifies a body focused repetitive behaviour, and habit reversal training combining awareness training with a competing response has the strongest evidence of any intervention. It is first line ahead of any medication in adolescents. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Recurrent hair pulling typically begins around puberty, affects girls more often than boys in clinical samples, and is frequently concealed for years by hairstyle changes. The diagnosis rests on the behavioural account rather than on the appearance of the scalp, though hairs of varying length within an irregular patch with normal underlying skin is the characteristic finding and separates it from autoimmune and infective causes. It sits with skin picking among the body focused repetitive behaviours, which differ from obsessive compulsive disorder in that the behaviour is preceded by tension or an urge rather than by an intrusive thought, and it responds to behavioural rather than serotonergic treatment. Swallowing the pulled hair occurs in a minority and carries a real risk of a gastric hair mass, so it must be asked about directly.
key_points: An urge with tension before and relief after defines the behaviour
Hairs of varying length within the patch indicate mechanical pulling
Normal scalp skin excludes fungal and autoimmune causes
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Ask directly about swallowing hair because of gastric mass risk
explanation.pearls: Around a fifth of people who pull also swallow the hair, and the resulting gastric mass can extend into the small bowel as a tail, so persistent abdominal pain with unexplained iron deficiency in a puller is a surgical presentation rather than a psychiatric one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to fall asleep before three in the morning on school nights who sleeps soundly until midday on holidays with normal total sleep time
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16 year old boy whose mother is worried that he is depressed because he cannot get out of bed for school and has been late eleven times this term. He lies awake until about three in the morning however early he goes to bed, then has to be dragged out at seven.

During the recent two week school holidays he went to sleep at about three and woke spontaneously at about eleven, felt refreshed and had no difficulty. His mood is good on weekends and in the holidays, he enjoys skateboarding and his appetite is normal. He drinks no caffeine after midday and does not use cannabis. His sleep diary shows a consistent sleep period of eight hours whenever he is allowed to choose the timing.

data_table.Examination: Alert with reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia described on direct questioning, no suicidal ideation, weight stable, general physical examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits, two week sleep diary showing sleep onset between 2:45 and 3:15 am with an eight hour sleep period when the wake time is unconstrained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start low dose melatonin timed several hours before his current sleep onset with morning light
options.rationale: A stable eight hour sleep period that is simply shifted later, with normal quality and refreshed waking when the timing is unconstrained, is a circadian phase problem rather than an inability to sleep. Small doses of melatonin given in the early evening shift the body clock earlier, and timed bright light after waking consolidates the shift. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.text: Start a sedating antidepressant at night and review his mood symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment addresses a depressive episode, which would show low mood and loss of interest across weekends and holidays as well as school days. His mood and enjoyment are intact whenever the timing constraint is removed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start temazepam at night for two weeks and taper it once his sleep pattern has settled
options.rationale: A hypnotic forces sleep onset without moving the underlying clock, so the pattern returns as soon as it is stopped, and benzodiazepines are not recommended for adolescents. His problem is the timing of the sleep period rather than an inability to sleep at all. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start a high dose of melatonin at his usual bedtime and continue it for at least three months
options.rationale: Melatonin shifts the clock through its timing rather than its sedative effect, so a large dose given at the current late bedtime acts as a hypnotic and can even delay the phase further. The near pair here is dose and timing, not the drug itself. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on any specific treatment approach
options.rationale: A sleep study answers questions about breathing, limb movements or unusual events during sleep, none of which are suggested here. His diary already demonstrates normal sleep duration and consolidation once the timing is free. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

explanation.summary: The circadian clock runs later during adolescence for biological reasons, and in a minority the shift is severe enough that sleep onset cannot be achieved before the early hours despite adequate opportunity. The diagnostic signature is a normal duration and quality of sleep whenever the timing is unconstrained, contrasted with severe difficulty on school days, which is why holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history. The pattern is regularly misread as depression, school refusal or laziness, and it does frequently produce secondary low mood, so the direction of causation must be teased out. Treatment combines evening melatonin at a low dose given well before current sleep onset, bright light exposure on waking, avoidance of evening screens and light, and gradual advancement of the schedule, with weekend consistency the hardest and most important element.
key_points: Normal sleep when timing is unconstrained separates this from insomnia
Holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history
Melatonin works by shifting phase, so timing matters more than dose
Morning bright light consolidates the advance in phase
Secondary low mood is common and resolves as the schedule corrects
explanation.pearls: Melatonin advances the body clock when taken about five hours before habitual sleep onset, so in an adolescent falling asleep at three in the morning the first dose belongs around ten at night, and giving it at the current bedtime wastes the phase shifting effect entirely.

sources.label: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people
Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

subtopic_detail: Older woman with two years of difficulty maintaining sleep requesting a repeat hypnotic after four weeks of temazepam with a normal screening for depression and sleep apnoea
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71 year old woman who has come in asking for another script for the sleeping tablet another doctor started a month ago. She wakes at about two each morning and lies there for two hours, and this has been going on for two years.

She says the tablet worked well for the first fortnight and now she needs it just to get the same sleep she had before. She is not low in mood, still plays bridge twice a week and gardens most days. Her husband says she does not snore and has never stopped breathing at night. She drinks one glass of wine with dinner and no coffee after lunch. She naps for an hour most afternoons in her armchair and is in bed by nine each night.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg per square metre, neck circumference 33 cm, Geriatric Depression Scale 2 out of 15, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30, no postural drop, gait steady with no aid
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current hypnotic at the same dose and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics are recommended for no more than two to four weeks, and continued use in an older person roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture while the hypnotic effect fades. She has already reached the recommended limit. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and plan a gradual hypnotic taper
options.rationale: Structured behavioural therapy including stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive work is first line for persistent insomnia at every age and produces benefits that persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics. Her rising dose requirement after two weeks is tolerance, which is the signal to plan withdrawal rather than to repeat the script. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.text: Switch to a sedating antihistamine at night and review her sleep pattern in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines carry a substantial anticholinergic burden that contributes to confusion, urinary retention and falls in older people, and tolerance to the sedation develops within days. Substituting one hypnotic for a worse one does not address the maintaining factors. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night for its sedating effect and review her sleep again in six weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants have a role when insomnia accompanies a depressive episode, and the near pair is that both approaches produce sleep, but only one is indicated without depression. Her depression screen is negative and she remains engaged and active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before making any change to her current medication
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when obstructive breathing, limb movements or parasomnia is suspected, signalled by snoring, witnessed apnoea, a large neck or unrefreshing sleep despite adequate duration. Her partner reports none of these and her neck circumference is small. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on at least three nights a week for three months with daytime consequences, and it is maintained by behaviours that develop in response to poor sleep rather than by whatever started it. Excessive time in bed, daytime napping and clock watching are the usual culprits, and they are precisely what behavioural therapy targets through stimulus control and sleep restriction. Australian guidance is unambiguous that psychological treatment is first line at all ages and that hypnotics are limited to short courses, because tolerance develops within weeks while the harms of falls, fracture, cognitive impairment and daytime sedation accumulate. Digital and telephone delivered programmes have made the therapy accessible outside metropolitan areas, which removes the commonest practical excuse for a repeat script.
key_points: Behavioural therapy is first line for chronic insomnia at any age
Benefits of therapy persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics
Hypnotics are limited to two to four weeks because of tolerance
Eleven hours in bed with an afternoon nap dilutes sleep pressure
Benzodiazepines roughly double fall and fracture risk in older people
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction that sets the time in bed to match actual sleep time, in her case about six hours with a fixed rise time, is the single most effective component of the therapy, and it usually worsens daytime sleepiness in the first fortnight before the improvement appears.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

subtopic_detail: Residual nightly trauma related nightmares with waking in a sweat after completing an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy that resolved the daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41 year old former soldier who completed sixteen sessions of trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy with an experienced psychologist four months ago. His avoidance, hypervigilance and intrusive daytime memories have largely resolved and he has returned to work full time.

What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes at about two in the morning from a dream replaying a specific incident, drenched in sweat and with his heart racing, then stays awake. His partner says he shouts but does not get out of bed or act out the dreams. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and no more. He takes no regular medication and his physical examination and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no current suicidal ideation, no postural blood pressure drop, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his treatment?

options.text: Start quetiapine at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics are widely prescribed for sleep in this population but Australian guidance does not support them as adjuncts, and they bring weight gain, metabolic change and sedation. They are considered only for treatment resistant illness under specialist supervision. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Start temazepam at night and review his nightmare frequency again in four weeks time
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in this condition because they suppress the emotional processing that psychological treatment depends on, worsen outcomes in several trials and carry dependence risk in a group with high comorbid substance use. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Repeat a second full course of trauma focused psychological therapy with a new therapist
options.rationale: A further course is reasonable when the daytime symptoms have failed to respond, whereas his avoidance and hypervigilance have largely resolved and only the nocturnal symptom persists. The near pair is that both options treat the same disorder but target different residual domains. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Start prazosin at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
options.rationale: Persisting trauma related nightmares after an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy are the recognised indication for adjunctive prazosin, which reduces noradrenergic activity during sleep and is titrated upward from a small night time dose. Postural blood pressure is checked as the dose rises. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Arrange polysomnography to look for a disorder of rapid eye movement sleep behaviour
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when the person physically enacts dreams, leaves the bed or injures a partner, which raises a parasomnia of later life. His partner reports shouting only, with no motor enactment. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance places trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for posttraumatic stress disorder, and most people who complete an adequate course improve substantially. Residual symptoms are common and it is worth identifying which domain persists, because the answer differs for daytime intrusions, avoidance, mood and sleep. Trauma related nightmares are among the most persistent symptoms and respond poorly to antidepressants alone, which is why an adjunctive noradrenergic blocker occupies a specific niche and imagery rehearsal therapy is offered where it is available. The evidence for prazosin is mixed, with a large negative trial in stable veterans alongside several positive studies, so it is used as a trial with a clear review point rather than as an open ended prescription, and blood pressure is monitored during titration.
key_points: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line, ahead of medication
Identify which symptom domain persists before adding anything
Nightmares respond poorly to antidepressant monotherapy
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are specifically discouraged
Dream enactment with movement suggests a parasomnia, not nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin is started at 1 mg at night because of first dose hypotension, and the postural blood pressure should be rechecked at each increase, with most responders settling between 3 mg and 10 mg nightly over several weeks of titration.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

subtopic_detail: Man presenting with debt and marital crisis after escalating sports betting with chasing of losses, no alcohol or drug use and no manic features
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 36 year old man who says his wife has told him to get help or leave. Over three years his sports betting has grown from a weekly bet to daily in play betting, and he has taken out a personal loan of 40000 dollars and borrowed from his brother without telling her.

He describes needing larger stakes for the same excitement, returning the next day to win back what he lost, and lying about how much he bets. He has tried to stop four times and lasted at most a fortnight. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He has never had a period of reduced sleep with elevated mood or overspending outside gambling. He denies current suicidal thoughts but says he has felt hopeless about the debt.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but well kempt, speech normal in rate and volume, mood described as flat with reactive affect, no grandiosity or pressured speech, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact, no signs of chronic liver disease or intravenous drug use
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start naltrexone at 50 mg daily and review his gambling and his mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in this condition and are considered when psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Medication is not the first intervention when structured therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start a mood stabiliser for an underlying bipolar disorder and review his mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Excessive gambling occurring only during periods of elevated mood, reduced sleep and other disinhibited spending would point to a mood disorder, and the near pair matters because both produce financial harm. His gambling has been continuous for three years with no elevated episodes. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling with financial counselling alongside
options.rationale: Tolerance to stake size, chasing losses, concealment and repeated failed attempts to stop define a behavioural addiction, and structured cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling related cognitions has the strongest evidence, delivered alongside financial counselling because unresolved debt is a powerful driver of relapse. Both are available free through Australian gambling help services. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer to a residential withdrawal unit for supervised abstinence over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Inpatient withdrawal exists to manage the physiological consequences of stopping a substance, and there is no physical withdrawal syndrome from gambling. Removing him from home for a fortnight does not address the cognitions or the debt that will greet him on return. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Advise him to self exclude from venues and review his gambling again in three months time
options.rationale: Self exclusion and blocking software are useful harm reduction measures and should be part of the plan, but used alone they leave the underlying cognitions untreated and online accounts are easily reopened. It is an adjunct rather than a treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance use disorders because it shares tolerance, loss of control, preoccupation, concealment and continuation despite harm, and Australians lose more per adult to gambling than any other population. Chasing losses is the most specific feature and distinguishes problem gambling from recreational betting more reliably than the amount wagered. Screening matters because affected people rarely raise it themselves and present instead with depression, anxiety, relationship breakdown, workplace theft or suicidal thinking, and suicide risk in this group is several times the background rate. Treatment centres on cognitive behavioural therapy addressing beliefs about luck, skill and near misses, combined with practical measures including self exclusion, account blocking and financial counselling, with family involvement where the person agrees.
key_points: Chasing losses is the most specific feature of disordered gambling
Screen for it when depression, debt or relationship crisis presents
Suicide risk is several times higher than in the general population
Cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling is the primary treatment
Financial counselling and self exclusion are adjuncts, not substitutes
explanation.pearls: Continuous forms such as in play sports betting and electronic gaming machines cause disproportionate harm compared with weekly lottery products, because the short interval between stake and outcome allows chasing within a single sitting.

subtopic_detail: Choice of relapse prevention pharmacotherapy after alcohol withdrawal in a man with compensated cirrhosis and normal renal function
stem:
You are the medical registrar planning discharge for a 54 year old man who completed a five day inpatient alcohol withdrawal with a diazepam loading regimen and has had no withdrawal signs for 48 hours. He has been drinking about 15 standard drinks daily for a decade and wants to stay abstinent.

He has cirrhosis diagnosed on transient elastography and ultrasound last year, with no ascites, no encephalopathy and no variceal bleeding, and his synthetic function is preserved. He takes no opioids and has no chronic pain. His renal function is normal. He is already booked with the drug and alcohol counsellor and his partner will attend with him. He has had no seizures during this or any previous withdrawal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Spider naevi over the upper chest, palmar erythema, liver edge firm and non-tender, no ascites on percussion, no asterixis, no jaundice, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 22 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin 37 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.2 (0.9-1.3), alanine aminotransferase 68 units per litre (less than 40), creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-450)

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medication should you start?

options.text: Naltrexone started now at the standard dose and continued for at least six months
options.rationale: Naltrexone is at least as effective for reducing heavy drinking days but undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is avoided in significant liver disease, and the near pair is that both are first line agents separated here purely by the organ that clears them. Liver function must also be monitored if it is ever used. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Disulfiram started now at the standard dose and continued with supervised administration
options.rationale: Disulfiram carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity and depends on a supervised aversive reaction, making it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. It is reserved for highly motivated people with normal liver function and a supervising partner. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Baclofen started now at a low dose and titrated upwards over the following several weeks
options.rationale: Baclofen is renally cleared and is sometimes used in advanced liver disease, but the evidence base is weaker and the Australian position places it as a second line option after the established agents. It also carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Diazepam continued at a tapering dose for a further month alongside counselling sessions
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat the withdrawal syndrome and are stopped once it has resolved, which happened 48 hours ago, and continuing them creates dependence while raising encephalopathy risk in cirrhosis. They have no relapse prevention role. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Acamprosate started now at the standard dose and continued for at least six months
options.rationale: Acamprosate is not metabolised by the liver and is cleared renally, so preserved synthetic function with normal creatinine makes it the appropriate choice in cirrhosis, and it is started immediately after withdrawal is complete. It reduces the risk of returning to any drinking. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy is offered to everyone with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder alongside psychosocial treatment, yet it remains substantially underprescribed in Australian practice. The two first line agents work differently, with acamprosate stabilising glutamatergic transmission to support ongoing abstinence and naltrexone blunting the rewarding effect of alcohol to reduce heavy drinking. The choice between them turns on organ function and on concurrent medication, since acamprosate is renally cleared and contraindicated in severe renal impairment, while naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is also incompatible with any opioid analgesia. Disulfiram remains an option for motivated people with supervision and normal liver function, and in all cases the medication is a support for counselling rather than a replacement for it.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally cleared and suits significant liver disease
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and blocked by opioid use
Disulfiram risks hepatotoxicity and needs supervised administration
Start relapse prevention as soon as withdrawal has resolved
Medication supplements rather than replaces psychosocial treatment
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate is contraindicated once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 30 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, so the practical rule is that the kidney decides for acamprosate and the liver decides for naltrexone.
